# Chapter 18 - sketch answers {.unnumbered}

\(1\) (a) Credential stuffing - broken by MFA (uniqueness would have prevented
it, MFA stops the login). (b) Phishing - live-relayed TOTP fails; only a
phishing-resistant factor (passkey) breaks it. (c) Guessing - broken by
breached-list/common-password screening plus length. (2) "Passwords: Passphrases
of at least 12--16 characters (length beats 8-plus-symbols); screened against
known-breached lists (removes what attackers try first); unique per system,
supported by the provided password manager (breaks stuffing); no scheduled
rotation - change on suspicion of compromise (rotation bred predictable
tweaks); account recovery via verified channels, no security questions
(public-answer passwords)." (3) (a) TOTP for customers: A large win over SMS at
negligible friction, proportionate to per-account value. (b) Passkeys for
admins: Their accounts are where phishing is aimed and where the blast radius
lives, so the factor must resist the one path ordinary MFA leaves open; the
split is @tbl-mfarank applied with Chapter 17's proportionality -
protection graded by consequence, not convenience. (4) First, credential
compromise - §18.1's uniqueness/stuffing failure (leaked contractor password).
Second, MFA-fatigue acceptance - §18.4's factor-quality failure: Push prompts
are phishable by persistence; number matching or passkeys close it. Third,
hardcoded privileged credentials on a share - §18.5's least-privilege and
privileged-account failure: The secret that turned one login into all of them.
(5) Risk: R3 - customer-database breach. Controls: Encryption at rest
(A.8.24); least-privilege database access with review (A.5.15/A.5.18); logging
and monitoring (A.8.15). Residual: Low--medium, was high inherent. Status:
Accepted by management, dated, per Chapter 17's row; KRI "privileged accounts
with direct database access" on the dashboard as the review trigger; revisit at
twelve months or on trigger.
